ctx.x: Well, we came into the Sherman Hotel around, I believe it was 1941. We were one of the first of a group of jazz artists that performed at the Panther Room and that was a room that they served the food on the flaming swords and such things as that, quite an elegant room. So, Lionel Hampton was the featured performer there with his orchestra and he had a supporting act there by the name of Billie Holliday. So, before we -- after we had rehearsals and right before we went into our beginning show that night, Lionel…

So, since I was standing up in front of the band and I announced her and brought her on the floor and I was the one that was leading the applause when she finished, I thought it no more than right that I should bring her back as many times as she warranted. Since Miss Billie Holliday was one of a kind in her particular type of singing, she warranted several encores, which I proceeded to give to her, for which I was roundly chewed out when I finished the night's performance by my band leader, Mr. Hampton.

items.title: Lionel Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: and then we had Marshall Royal, who was a great saxophone player

ctx.x: I tell you, I was always lucky. Because I was always seeking the fine youngsters, you know. They want to be musicians, and was waiting for a break to play in a big band. Because big bands was very popular then, just like when I left Benny Goodman and went out to get my band, there was little kids walking around in California, where I was staying at, after I left Benny Goodman, he took sick. And the doctors who were at the place warned him not to play no more for six months, because he had a disease called…

the clarinet. Well I told him I said “I want you to play tenor.” So finally my wife, my late wife, Gladys, had got a guy and went down to the [sounds like] Lucky Music Company. That’s where all the musicians traded with, and gave him a tenor saxophone, and then we had Marshall Royal, who was a great saxophone player. Marshall, when his brother was coming up, Ernie Royal, Ernie Royal could play really high notes on trumpet.
Did you put him on lead then?
